description: Halve any recipe without the awkward fractions. Every ingredient times 0.5, eggs handled whole or beaten, and small amounts in spoons you can measure.

examples.result: The halved pasta sauce serves 2: 1 cup tomatoes, 1/2 cup onion, 1 clove garlic, 1 tablespoon oil.
steps: Multiply each amount by 0.5: 2 cups tomatoes become 1 cup, 1 cup onion becomes 1/2 cup.
Garlic: 2 cloves × 0.5 = 1 clove. Oil: 2 tablespoons × 0.5 = 1 tablespoon.
examples.title: A pasta sauce for 4, halved to serve 2

examples.result: The halved muffins use 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup sugar, 1 egg, and 1 teaspoon baking powder.
steps: Flour: 2 cups × 0.5 = 1 cup. Sugar: 1 cup × 0.5 = 1/2 cup.
Eggs: 2 × 0.5 = 1 egg. Baking powder: 2 teaspoons × 0.5 = 1 teaspoon.
examples.title: A dozen muffins, halved to make 6

faqs.answer: Beat one egg in a small bowl and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons. On a scale, half a large egg is about 25 g. For cookies and scones you can also just use the whole egg and reduce the other liquid slightly, but the beaten half is the reliable way.
faqs.question: How do you halve one egg?

faqs.answer: Yes, halving leavening is straightforward. Half the baking powder or soda exactly. The caution about leavening applies to scaling up, not down.
faqs.question: Do you halve the baking powder too?

faqs.answer: Use a pan about half the area of the original, so the depth stays the same. A halved cake in the original pan bakes thin and dries out. An 8 inch square pan is a good stand in for a halved 9 by 13.
faqs.question: What size pan do I use for a halved recipe?

faqs.answer: A little less, usually. A smaller amount of food in a smaller pan cooks faster. Start checking about 5 minutes before the original time, and trust doneness tests over the clock.
faqs.question: Does a halved recipe cook faster?

faqs.answer: Convert to spoons. A third of a cup halved is 2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons, which you can measure. A quarter teaspoon halved is an eighth of a teaspoon, which is a pinch. The table above gives the spoon versions of the common amounts.

faqs.answer: For most dishes, yes. Halving is kinder than doubling, because nothing overflows and nothing over-leavens. The only recipes that resist halving are ones built around a whole item, like a whole chicken or a whole cake layer, where the shape matters.

formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. Halving means a factor of 0.5.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 2 has a factor of 0.5.

howToSteps.name: Halve each amount
howToSteps.text: Work down the ingredient list and multiply each amount by 0.5. Cups halve cleanly, and the table above gives the spoon versions of the awkward ones.

howToSteps.name: Deal with the eggs
howToSteps.text: An even number of eggs halves cleanly. An odd number leaves a half egg: beat one egg and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons.

howToSteps.name: Halve the leavening too
howToSteps.text: Baking powder and baking soda halve exactly. Unlike scaling up, there is no adjustment needed when you scale down.

howToSteps.name: Use a smaller pan
howToSteps.text: Pick a pan about half the area so the depth stays the same. Check for doneness a little early, because a smaller batch cooks faster.

title: How to Halve a Recipe: Cut It in Half
tutorial: Halving is the kindest scaling there is. Nothing overflows, nothing over-leavens, and the factor is 0.5, which is easy maths. A recipe for 4 becomes a recipe for 2. Two cups of flour become 1. One cup of stock becomes half a cup. It is the scaling I do most often, because most recipes serve four and most weeknight tables do not.

The awkward part is not the maths, it is the measuring. A third of a cup halved is a sixth of a cup, and no measuring cup has a sixth. The fix is to think in spoons: a sixth of a cup is 2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons, which you can measure exactly. A quarter teaspoon halved is an eighth of a teaspoon, which is a pinch. The table above gives the spoon versions of the common amounts, so you never have to guess.

Eggs are the one ingredient that needs a decision. An even number halves cleanly: 2 eggs become 1, 4 become 2. An odd number leaves a half egg, and the reliable way to handle it is to beat one egg in a small bowl and use half of it, about 1 1/2 tablespoons. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, so half is about 25 g if you would rather weigh it.

Unlike doubling, halving needs no leavening adjustment. Baking powder and baking soda halve exactly, and salt and spices halve exactly too. What changes is the pan: use one about half the area of the original, so the depth stays the same. A halved cake in the original pan bakes thin and dries out. And check for doneness early, because a smaller batch cooks a little faster.

Halving is also a good way to test a new recipe before you commit to the full batch. Make half, see if it is worth making again, and if it is, you already know the full amounts. If you halve a big batch-cooking recipe instead of cooking the whole thing, the half you do not cook keeps better as raw ingredients than as leftovers, so store the ingredients, not the extra dinner.
